# OA.3 The rich economies with the design given {#oecd}

Section 6 of the paper calibrates the model without informal households to the U.S., France and the UK, and
imposes on the U.S. the characteristics that set France apart; appendices E to G give the data and the household
heterogeneity behind the calibration, the results under CRRA preferences, and the same counterfactuals with the UK
as host. This chapter
holds all of them, each under both calibrations of the taste for leisure, and the calibrations at every IES of the
model's grid.

## OA.3.1 Calibration {#oecd-calibration}

The country parameters, with those the three countries share in a lower panel, and, by income group, the population shares, the taste for leisure, the productivities and
the propensities to vote. France is grouped at the U.S. income percentiles and, for the UK as host, at the UK's.
The UK is also regrouped at the U.S. percentiles for one row of the paper's cross-country test in section 7; that
regrouping is a linear fit of the UK's own group means against their cumulative population shares, not a recount
of the survey.

## OA.3.2 The vector-$X_i$ calibration {#oecd-vectorx}

The paper identifies each income group's productivity and taste for leisure by taking the taste for leisure common
across groups and fixing its level by the average workweek, so that relative hours are a prediction. The
alternative takes the observed relative hours as data as well, which identifies one $X_i$ per group and leaves the
level of hours unidentified. The productivity distribution reaches every aggregate only through
$\sum_i \gamma_i \eta_i^{1+\xi}/X_i^{\xi}$, which both calibrations normalize to one, so the calibration is block
recursive: what depends on the design or on the demography is the same under both, and only what is defined
through $\eta_i$ or $X_i$ separately can move. The table compares every exhibit that exists under both
calibrations, cell by cell; on each exhibit, the calibration switch and *mark the cells that differ* show the same
comparison in place.

## OA.3.3 The calibration across the intertemporal elasticity {#oecd-rhogrid}

The parameters solved jointly with the equilibrium path at every IES of the grid, for each country. Sections 6 and
7 explain the CRRA results by how the calibration absorbs a higher IES; these are the numbers behind that
explanation.

## OA.3.4 Counterfactuals on the U.S. {#oecd-us}

The paper's overview figure of section 6 collects the effect of each counterfactual on the tax rate, the savings
rate and the workweek at three values of the IES. The tables print them: at the paper's benchmark, with the
economic-equilibrium effect beside the full one, and at each IES. Click a bar for its row.

## OA.3.5 The UK as host {#oecd-uk}

The counterfactuals of section 6 on the UK's own calibration: France's characteristics, with France's households
regrouped at the UK's income percentiles, and the pension design and ageing at each IES. The figure sets the two
hosts side by side for France's characteristics; the tables print the UK's numbers.
